T-87. Stiff-Man Syndrome: Clinical Course, Treatments
and Outcomes
Maisha T. Robinson, Sean J. Pittock,
Vanda A. Lennon, J. Eric Ahlskog,
Kathleen M. Mc Evoy, Joseph Y. Matsumoto,
and Andrew Mc Keon; Rochester, MN
Stiff-man syndrome (SMS, Moersch-Woltman syndrome) is
characterized by lumbar and lower extremity muscle stiffness
and superimposed spasms. We describe clinical course, treatments and outcomes in this chart review and longitudinal
telephone study of 60 Mayo Clinic patients with classical
SMS (1984-2008). Median age of symptom-onset was 40
years (range, 7-70); 2 had childhood-onset. 73% were
women. 95% were GAD65 autoantibody seropositive (median value, 623 nmol/L; range, 0. 05-8620 [normal value,
0. 02 nmol/L]). 18% developed additional neurological
disorders (epilepsy, 8%; ataxia, 7%; parkinsonism, 3%).
66% had 1 coexisting autoimmune disease: diabetes mellitus, 47%; thyroid disease, 31%; pernicious anemia, 8%; vitiligo, 5%; Addison’s disease, 3%. Cancer was uncommon
(7%). Of 34 patients with surveillance 5 years, 59%
received immunotherapy (1 of IVIg, corticosteroids,
plasma exchange, azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil);
improvements were reported in 86%. Disability measures
among those who received immunotherapies were similar to
those who did not. All continued symptomatic treatments
including benzodiazepines (median diazepam dose, 30mg/
day). Median Rankin score after 5 years was 2 (range, 05); 70% could walk unaided. SMS patients commonly have
coexisting organ-specific autoimmunity. Ongoing therapies
(symptomatic þ/- immunotherapy) are required for symptomatic relief with most walking independently in the longterm.
